author_response_spans.text: We thank the reviewer for their suggestion to clarify the meaning of the title “Diminishing Returns of Reservoir Construction”. There is an implied simplification involved with using the word "return". We are using the word "return" in the same way as the phrase "return on investment". In other words, the "return" (or benefit) of constructing new reservoirs, as defined by NS, has declined. Of course there are other benefits to building reservoirs (e.g., flood reduction, recreation), as well as costs (environmental, social), but we are framing the returns in terms of water storage. To provide more clarification, we have changed the title to “Diminishing Storage Returns of Reservoir Construction”, and modified the following sentence in the manuscript: “While the new reservoirs have led to a steadily increasing global storage capacity, their returns are diminished (i.e., their NS is lower) compared to those built in the 20[th] century.” (Lines 70-71).

Our finding about the decreasing NS values of new reservoirs is based on a comparison of the NS values of old and new reservoirs in the same basin, while assuming that climatology conditions within a basin were homogeneous. So it is reasonable to state that “The reservoirs constructed in the 21[st] century have smaller NS values and larger seasonal variations than those built earlier, suggesting they are more susceptible to droughts.”. In addition, we changed the term “returns” to “storage returns” for clarification: “With predicted decreasing runoff and increasing water demand, these observed diminishing storage returns of reservoir construction will likely persist into the future.” (Lines 23-25), “The contrasting storage and NS trends indicate that the recent storage returns of global reservoir construction have been declining since the start of the 21[st] century.” (Lines 100-102), “The results from this study highlight the challenges of resolving finite water resources through reservoir regulations, particularly in developing countries where the storage returns from these impoundments are diminishing.” (Lines 206-209).
## Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

The authors have carefully addressed my previous comments. I reiterate the value of this study. However, while I appreciate that the authors added caveats regarding sedimentation, the analysis and additional elements provided in response to my comments and that of the other reviewer warrant adjustment.
First, P20L362 “Despite the impacts of sedimentation on the absolute reservoir storage, the conclusions based on the normalized storage (NS) results are not affected. This is because

sedimentation tends to reduce the actual storage (numerator) and storage capacity (denominator) equally, so the NS is not much affected.” Although the statement that NS is unaffected is valid, this strict definition of NS (using current storage capacity rather than initial storage capacity as the denominator) is of little relevance for management. What really matters for water provision and hydroelectric production for example, is actual storage/initial storage capacity. Therefore, I suggest removing this argument.
Thanks for this comment. We have removed this statement.

Second, I question the choice of reservoirs for illustrating the impact of sedimentation. How were these reservoirs chosen? The annual sedimentation rates, which range between 0.025 and 0.253%/year are on the very low range compared to global averages. The following paragraph from Wisser et al. (2013) illustrates this point : “A global data set with consistently measured sediment volumes trapped in reservoirs over time is not available, and, in fact there has been a decline in the collection of sedimentation data [Syvitski, 2003; Vanmaercke et al., 2011b]. For the US, the Reservoir Sedimentation Database (RESSED) [Ackermann et al., 2009] provides statistics on reservoir volumes derived from bathymetric surveys for more than 1800 reservoirs from which sedimentation loss rates can be calculated (using successive surveys). We calculated sedimentation rates of 1024 reservoirs with at least two complete surveys (using the most recent surveys) and supplemented this data set with observed loss rates from an additional 191 reservoirs globally from a variety of sources (Figure 1) to get a global sample of observed loss rates.This data set covers a wide range of physical conditions in the catchment (e.g., slope, climate, soil type, and land use) and local reservoir conditions (size, area, bathymetry, purpose, and management practices). Observed loss rates vary between 0.0017% a−1 and 36% a−1 and are 1.35% a−1 on average (median = 0.55% a−1). Loss rates for reservoirs with a capacity larger than the minimum capacity in the GRanD database (1 million m3) have lower loss rates (mean = 0.76% a−1, median 0.35% a−1; Table 1). Weighted by initial capacity, the mean loss rate is 0.66%.

Out of fifty reservoirs in Italy, Patro et al. (2022) mention “According to the latest report of the International Commission On Large Dams (ICOLD, 2009), the global average value for sedimentation rate (and so storage loss) is around 0.96%.” and find mean annual sedimentation rates of 0.57% and a total mean loss of reservoir capacity of 37%.

These points do not lessen the merit of this study but must be properly acknowledged. Sedimentation is a widespread phenomenon in reservoirs that surely has, on aggregate, more long-term impact on storage capacity than the changes observed by this study.
Thanks for pointing this out. In the previous response, we randomly selected four reservoirs with available sediment rate values from the Duke Nicholas Institute

(https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/reservoir-national-trends/sediment). This database provides sediment rate data for 150 U.S. reservoirs, and 100 of them are included in our dataset—which were selected to further evaluate the effects of sedimentation on the NS trend values. The sediment rate values of these reservoirs range from 0 to 18.18 %/year, with mean and median values of 1.37 and 0.70 %/year, respectively—which are close to the values in the abovereferences mentioned by the reviewer. Figure R3 shows the distribution of the sediment values, with over half of the reservoirs having sediment rates below 1 %/year.

About sedimentation impact on reservoir water level and area. I would like to thank the authors for looking into the literature and consulting Dagmar Llewellyn in the Bureau of Reclamation. I accept this rebuttal. Since potential readers may have similar concerns, I highly recommend that the authors include a similar discussion in the paper (in either the main text or methods) to echo this rebuttal.

For example, the authors can briefly discuss: (1) how reservoir management may respond to sedimentation (in most cases, sedimentation does not allow for water to be stored higher, with the exception of some of the flood-control reservoirs), and (2) how this response implies to the validity of the authors’ methods and conclusions (as sediment accumulates, the reservoir storage capacity may just decrease under the same water area, leading to limited impacts on the NS). Thanks for this comment. We have added discussion in the Methods section about the impact of sedimentation on reservoir water level and area changes (Lines 367-376): “Although sedimentation can reduce storage capacity, reservoir management does not allow for water to be stored higher due to concerns about dam safety. One rare exception is when a flood control reservoir has a recreation pool for which a certain volume of water is required to be maintained, and the surface level (of this required volume) is well below the elevation at capacity. In this

case, sedimentation can increase the surface area required to store the specified amount of water. Flushing or dredging is usually applied for mitigating the sedimentation effects on storage. In this study, our method relies on using surface area to infer the storage and does not consider the sedimentation effects. If the sedimentation amount is notable in a reservoir, then both the storage and storage capacity can be overestimated. However, based on the evaluation below, sedimentation has a limited effect on the NS values and the NS trends.”
The new text focuses on point (1).  For point (2), we have included a detailed explaination that addresses the observed sedimentation data (Lines 377-393).

About validation of the NS trends. It seems the NS trends derived from the simulation method are overall comparable with the trends from the bathymetry-based method. Although there are some disagreement and variability, the mean bias between the two methods appears low. I think this is a positive message. I highly recommend the authors add this validation (with Figure R1) to the paper (such as in “Evaluation of storage estimation” section), because given the focus here, validating NS trends is just as important as validating storage capacities. As another (optional) suggestion: If I were the authors, I would also try to absorb the validation statistics (such as the RMSE in Figure R1) to the uncertainties of the NS trend estimates for at least the 347 GRBD reservoirs.

Thanks for this comment. We have added language about this validation and a new figure (Supplementary Fig. 7) to the “Evaluation of storage estimation” section (Lines 345-349), “In addition, we compared the NS trend values derived from the simulation method with the results from bathymetry-based methods for the 347 global reservoirs. Supplementary Fig. 7 shows that the NS trend values derived from these two methods show good agreement (R[2] = 0.76), with the majority of the data aligning with the 1:1 line (with a slope value of 0.99).”
As the NS trends are primarily evaluated at large scales in this study, we have used the validation statistics in Supplementary Fig. 5 to assess the uncertainties of the NS trends.

About reservoir water area at capacity (Ao). It is good to see the authors have performed this sensitivity test and the difference between the estimated capacities using 95% Ao and those using 100% Ao appears limited based on the 277 reservoirs with in-situ storage. This is encouraging. To further secure this very important aspect, I am wondering if the authors can expand this
sensitivity analysis to other reservoirs, in order to inform the potential impact of inconsistent use of Ao on the conclusions about pre- and post-1999 NS.

For example, I suggest the following scheme for the sensitivity analysis (which should be straightforward to implement): (1) for the subset of pre-1999 reservoirs using 95% water occurrence as Ao, replace their Ao by 100% water occurrence, (2) for the subset of post-1999 reservoirs using 95% water occurrence as Ao, keep their Ao as they are (basically do nothing for post-1999 reservoirs), and (3) compare how much difference this inconsistent use of Ao will cause for the calculated pre-1999 and post-1999 NS values. This design should, in theory, report the maximum impact of Ao. As a reminder, the authors may need to re-simulate the geometric models for some of the pre-1999 reservoirs because their Ao is changed. I also recommend that the authors include such a sensitivity analysis in the method section, which will secure to readers that this aspect won’t affect the main conclusions of the paper.

The 100-percentile areas were not selected because these values may correspond to flooding circumstances, which can lead to overestimated water area values at capacity. ## Article 

## Diminishing storage returns of reservoir construction 

Received: 12 November 2022 Yao Li 1,4, Gang Zhao 2,5, George H. Allen 3 & Huilin Gao 1 Accepted: 17 May 2023 Surface water reservoirs are increasingly being relied upon to meet rising demands in the context of growing population and changing climate. HowCheck for updates ever, the amount of water available in reservoirs (and the corresponding trends) have not been well quantified at the global scale. Here we use satellite observations to estimate the storage variations of 7245 global reservoirs from 1999 to 2018. Total global reservoir storage has increased at a rate of 27.82 ± 0.08 km[3] /yr, which is mainly attributed to the construction of new — dams. However, the normalized reservoir storage (NS) the ratio of the actual — storage to the storage capacity has declined by 0.82 ± 0.01%. The decline of NS values is especially pronounced in the global south, while the global north mainly exhibits an NS increase. With predicted decreasing runoff and increasing water demand, these observed diminishing storage returns of reservoir construction will likely persist into the future. 

Although global reservoirs have a much smaller total capacity compared to natural lakes, their flow regulation represents the most intensive human-induced alteration of the hydrological cycle[1][–][5] . The 20th Century witnessed a massive dam construction boom, first starting in North America and then spreading to the rest of the inhabited world. Behind these dams, sprawling reservoirs have fundamentally enhanced our ability to manage Earth’s freshwater resources[6][–][8] , but have also imposed adverse environmental and social effects[9][–][13] .

After a decline in growth during the 1990s[14] , hundreds of large new dams have been added in Asia, Africa, and South America[3] . In addition, over 3700 hydropower dams (each over 1 MW in capacity) are being planned or are under construction as of 2014, most of which are in developing countries[15] . With water scarcity intensified by both climate change[16][–][19] and increasing water demand[20] , reservoir water availability is essential for sustainable development[21] . Yet dam construction and reservoir operations are rarely coordinated amongst countries despite nearly half of all land being covered by international river basins[22] . To best inform future decision-making related to global surface water management, the storage conditions of reservoir impoundments—particularly those — newly constructed should be carefully evaluated. 

However, knowledge about the long-term variation of reservoir storage is very limited at a global scale. In situ measurements of reservoir storage are often not shared, especially across international river basins[23] . Land-surface and hydrologic models produce highly uncertain storage estimates, largely due to the lack of reservoir operations/management information[24][–][26] . By relating reservoir surface area and elevation values, satellite remote sensing provides a viable alternative for monitoring storage[27][–][31] . Although recent studies have quantified long-term surface area time series values and seasonal elevation variations of reservoirs globally[5][,][32] , reliable storage estimations have only focused on reservoirs built before 1999 (hereafter referred to as “pre-1999 reservoirs”)[27][–][31] .

Here, we develop the Global Reservoir Storage (GRS) dataset to evaluate the conditions of global reservoir impoundments—particularly reservoirs constructed after 1999 (hereafter referred to as “post1999 reservoirs”). We built GRS using multi-source satellite data by converting monthly reservoir water areas from the Global Reservoir Surface Area Dataset (GRSAD)[32] to monthly storage values using bathymetric maps[33] and, where necessary, an improved bathymetry simulation method[34] (see “Methods”). ## Results and discussion 

We introduce “normalized storage” (NS), a new term defined as the ratio of the actual storage from a group of reservoirs to the storage capacity of these same reservoirs. The NS offers a unique flexibility for quantifying and comparing the storage returns of impoundment from different groups of reservoirs across global, continental, and basin scales. This makes regions with different storage capacities comparable, and it is not affected by the increased storage from new reservoirs. The use of NS allows us to: (1) split the pre- and post-1999 reservoirs and directly evaluate the behaviors of newly constructed reservoirs; (2) compare the NS trends with the actual storage trends for 

new insights; and (3) assess reservoirs grouped by different functionalities (e.g., hydropower, irrigation). 

While the newly constructed reservoirs have contributed to a steady increase in global storage capacity, their storage returns (in terms of NS) are found to be smaller than those built in the 20th – century (over the period of 1999 2018). The NS values of the post-1999 reservoirs are significantly lower (and with larger seasonal variations) than the pre-1999 ones, at 60.59 ± 4.33% and 70.36 ± 1.36%, respectively (Fig. 1b). The NS values also depend on reservoir function. For instance, the NS values in reservoirs whose primarily function is hydropower are generally higher than those whose primarily function is irrigation or flood control. Therefore, we further compared the NS values for pre-1999 and post-1999 reservoirs in terms of reservoir function, at both global and basin scales.

Regardless of the function — and/or spatial scale, all results lead to the same conclusion that post1999 reservoirs have lower NS levels, but larger seasonal variations, than pre-1999 reservoirs (Fig. 2). It is worth noting that there are many social-economic benefits to building reservoirs (e.g., hydropower generation, flood reduction, water supply, and recreation), but here we are framing the returns only in terms of normalized water storage.

## Methods 

## Reservoir storage estimation 

To estimate the time series of reservoir storage variations, we used the reservoir list/information, the surface area, and the Area-Storage (A-V) relationships. 

We extracted the information for 7245 reservoirs from the Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD)[3] (latest version v1.3). GRanD documents geospatially referenced dams and their associated reservoirs (larger than 0.1 km[3] ). GRanD also provides multiple attributes, such as dam height and length, reservoir area, and reservoir storage. The recently released GRanD v1.3 contains 7320 records, with a cumulative reservoir storage capacity of 6811 km[3] . Note that some dams are not associated with reservoirs. We assessed the storage variations for the 7245 reservoirs, which account for a total capacity of 6658 km[3] . There are 57 reservoirs in GRanD without reported storage capacity values. The capacity values for these were estimated based on empirical relationships established in Lehner et al.[3] . However, we found that this did not significantly impact the findings of this study (by comparing the results between including and excluding these reservoirs). Note that this study did not include a comprehensive census of the world’s reservoirs, especially with regard to the very small reservoirs. The GlObal geOreferenced Database of Dams (GOODD) provides the locations of 38,667 dams, but the associated reservoir shapes and other attributes are not available[43] . Lehner et al.[3] estimate that there were approximately 2000 km[3] more reservoirs (mainly small reservoirs) than the 6197 km[3] included in GRanD v1.1 (as of early 2011).

Couto and Olden[44] reveal that 82,891 small hydropower plants (SHPs) are being operated or are under construction—but their analysis is at the nation scale, and georeferenced location information for the individual SHPs are not accessible. Malerba et al.[45] detected 

1.765 million farm dams that occupy a volume of 10.99 km[3] . It has been estimated that the cumulative reservoir storage capacity is around 7000–8300 km[3][1][,][3][,][43][,][46] , and GRanD accounts for about 83% of this. 

We adopted the surface area time series values for these reservoirs from the Global Reservoir Surface Area Dataset (GRSAD)[32] . — Leveraging the Landsat-based Global Surface Water (GSW) dataset[47] which contains Earth’s monthly surface water maps at a 30 m resolution from 1984 to 2018—GRSAD corrected the underestimations due to image contamination (e.g., clouds and ice/snow) using a novel algorithm. However, this algorithm cannot be applied to images when more than 95% of the reservoir area is contaminated. Under these conditions, the missing monthly reservoir area values were filled in by a linear interpolation. It should be noted that, although Landsat observations for areas such as the United States and Australia are sufficient for seasonal and interannual evaluations from the early 1980s onward, the coverage for other regions is relatively low before the launch of Landsat-7 in 1999[48][–][50] . Therefore, the seasonal and interannual variations of reservoir storage were analyzed starting from 1999 in this study. 

The monthly storage time series were generated by applying GRSAD area estimations to the A-V relationships for the 7245 reservoirs. The A-V relationships were adopted from two sources.

The first is the high-resolution Global Reservoir Bathymetry Dataset (GRBD)[33] , which provides A-V relationships for 347 global artificial reservoirs. By combining the Surface Water Occurrence (SWO) images from GSW with lidar/radar altimetry data, the Area-Elevation (A-E) relationships were first derived for each reservoir. Then, the A-E relationships were, in turn, applied to the corresponding SWO images to obtain the bathymetry values. From the 3-D bathymetric maps, the A-V relationships were then derived[51] . 

The other source is a new A-V dataset produced by modifying a simulation method developed by Yigzaw et al.[34] , which was used for the 6898 reservoirs not included in GRBD. The modification was made in two aspects. First, we improved upon the representation of the reservoir areas at capacity. Yigzaw et al.[34] assumed that the polygon areas in GRanD represented the surface areas at storage capacity. However, the reservoir polygons were primarily based on information from the static Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) DEM collected in February of 2000—a period when most reservoirs were unlikely to be at their peaks (because of low fill, a dry season, or some other factors). To minimize this kind of uncertainty, we calculated the 95th percentile area value for each reservoir from the GRSAD dataset, and compared it with the associated area provided in GRanD. The larger value of the two was then selected to represent the area at capacity (for each given reservoir). A total of 5152 reservoir records were updated to the 95th percentile area values. Second, we combined each reservoir’s vertical and bottom profile shapes to estimate the area at each layer by scaling to the area at capacity (i.e., the top layer area).

Yigzaw et al.[34] used the effective length and width of the reservoirs, but did not consider the fact that the complexity of the surface shapes may lead to large uncertainties. We selected three possible bottom profile shapes—parabolic, linear, and square root—and used them in combination with four vertical profile shapes—prism, bowl, wedge, and concave wedge—to obtain twelve different reservoir geometries to choose from. A diagram of a reservoir geometry with a parabolic bottom profile and a prism vertical profile is shown in Supplementary Fig. 3a, with the corresponding parameters denoted in Supplementary Fig. 3b. The selected vertical and bottom profile shapes are shown in Supplementary Figs. 3c and 3d, respectively. 

The simulation method included two steps: First, the optimal geometry was determined for each reservoir. The total storage value was calculated for each of the twelve possible geometries by integrating the area with respect to the depth. Then the geometry with the estimated total storage closest to the reported capacity value in GRanD was selected as the optimal geometry. Second, for a given area value,

To further evaluate the performance of the two storage estimation methods, we used the simulation method to derive the A-E relationships for these same 49 reservoirs, and then compared the estimated storage values. Supplementary Fig. 6 shows that the estimated storage values from the two methods are in overall good agreement with the observations. ## Sources of uncertainty 

The storage dataset is associated with uncertainties primarily from two sources. The first is uncertainty due to reservoir sedimentation, which can reduce the storage capacity[52] . Reservoir sedimentation is affected by several major factors, such as geometry, streamflow, sediment load, particle size, deposit-specific weight, reservoir size, and operation rules[53][–][55] . It has been reported that the sedimentation rate varies with reservoir size, with the larger reservoirs having smaller rates[56][–][58] . Recently, Wisser et al.[58] evaluated the storage capacity loss for global reservoirs in GRanD. Their analysis shows that the total storage capacity declined by 4.5% from 1990 to 2010, at an annual rate of 0.23%. Moreover, Dendy et al.[57] estimated the average annual loss rates for a series of different size categories using the sedimentation data for 1105 reservoirs.

Based on the set of loss rates obtained from Dendy et al.[57] , we calculated the annual storage sedimentation values for each reservoir included in the GRS dataset. Then, the total storage sedimentation was divided by the total storage capacity to estimate the — annual storage sedimentation rate 0.18%. Currently, a wide range of techniques (e.g., flushing and dredging) have been developed and implemented to control sedimentation, and to ensure the long-term sustainability of the reservoirs[55][,][59][–][61] . It should be noted that a fraction of the reservoirs in our dataset (e.g., some in the U.S. and India) were evaluated in terms of live storage, which is more resistant to sedimentation. 

Although sedimentation can reduce storage capacity, reservoir management does not allow for water to be stored higher than planned due to concerns about dam safety. One rare exception is when a flood-control reservoir has a recreation pool for which a certain volume of water is required to be maintained, and the surface level

## Comparisons with other storage datasets available at a global scale 

A number of remotely sensed global reservoir storage datasets have been developed since the early 2010s[27][–][31] . All of these datasets are based on using the A-E relationships to estimate the reservoir and/or lake storage variations. The main difference between them is the source of the satellite data. For example, Busker et al.[29] combined the GSW dataset and the satellite altimetry database DAHITI—Database for Hydrological Time Series over Inland Waters—to establish the A-E relationships, which provide long-term storage variation values for 137 lakes and reservoirs. Comparisons of A-E relationships in Busker et al.[29] with ours show similar quality[33] . Tortini et al.[30] used MODIS-based water surface areas and a satellite radar altimetry dataset to establish A-E relationships for 347 global lakes and reservoirs.

In general, the MODIS-based reservoir storage estimations have larger errors and uncertainties than those of Landsat-based estimations[31] . In addition, the Busker et al.[29] and Tortini et al.[30] datasets provide the time series of storage variations (i.e., change in storage) rather than absolute storage values.

We used the ratio of the total water storage in all of the reservoirs relative to the total storage capacity for a geographical domain (i.e., global, continental, and river basin scales) to calculate the normalized storage. In this way, the NS can be used as an overall indicator of the relative storage variations at large scales. Note that we did not use the average value of the NS for all of the reservoirs (with each reservoir having equal weight). This is because it is a mathematical average primarily determined by the NS of the large amount small reservoirs

The storage values during the impoundment periods of new reservoirs could impact the NS values. For the remainder of the reservoirs, we used a semi-manual method to identify their impoundment periods. We compared the NS values for global pre- and post-1999 reservoirs in terms of reservoir function. Figure 2a shows that post-1999 reservoirs tend to be designed for hydropower purposes (vs. pre-1999 ones; 80.9% vs. 63.6%), but less for irrigation (7.8% vs. 19.9%) and flood control (3.4% vs. 6.9%). The NS values for post-1999 reservoirs are lower (with larger seasonal variations) than pre-1999 reservoirs (Fig. 2b–d) for all of the reservoir functions—hydropower (63.65 ± 4.66% vs. 71.37 ± 1.84%), irrigation (52.39 ± 8.53% vs. 60.83 ± 2.88%), and flood control (50.98 ± 6.71% vs. 56.90 ± 3.09%). At the continental scale, the locations of pre- and post1999 reservoirs may play a role, because of the heterogeneous climatology within the continent. Thus, we conducted the comparison— taking the reservoir function into consideration—at the basin scale, assuming that the climatology conditions within a basin were homogeneous. We only selected basins that have at least five post-1999 reservoirs with the same primary function, such that the NS values would not be biased by a small number of samples. A total of ten basins were identified that met this criterion.

Results show that, in nine out of the ten basins studied, the mean NS values of post-1999 reservoirs are lower than those of pre-1999 reservoirs—with the exception of post1999 reservoirs used for irrigation purposes in the India-South basin (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 1). With regard to mean annual CV values, the pre- and post-1999 reservoirs used for irrigation in the same basins have similar seasonal variations (Supplementary Table 1). However, post-1999 reservoirs with hydropower as their primary purpose exhibit greater seasonal variation than pre-1999 (hydropower focused) reservoirs—except for those in the Parana basin (Supplementary Table 1). Thus, these comparisons indicate that post-1999 reservoirs have lower NS levels—but larger seasonal variations—than pre-1999 ones. 

## Trend analysis of storage and NS time series 

We adopted the scheme developed by Pascolini-Campbell et al.[62] to evaluate the trends of storage and NS time series. First, the seasonal cycle was removed using the climatology values, and then a moving average of 15 months was applied to obtain the interannual variability of the anomaly time series. Then, the non-parametric Mann-Kendall significance test[63][,][64] was used to statistically assess if there was a monotonic upward or downward trend of storage (or NS) over time (with α = 0.05). Finally, the Theil-Sen slope estimator[65][,][66] was employed to detect the linear trend of storage (or NS) time series. Note that the first and last seven monthly values of the time series were not used for the trend analysis. 

## Analysis of potential drivers of NS patterns 

We analyzed the potential drivers of the NS patterns at the basin scale, which included runoff, population density, and reservoir use.

The runoff data were provided by the GLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 monthly 0.25 × 0.25 degree V2.1 (GLDAS_NOAH025_M 2.1) product from 2000 to 2018[67] . We calculated the long-term mean runoff value for each basin that contained the studied reservoirs. The gridded population density data were collected from the Gridded Population — of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4) data sets which provide an estimate of population density for the years 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020 (https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/gpw-v4-populationdensity-adjusted-to-2015-unwpp-country-totals-rev11). We used the average value from these five years to represent the population density for each basin. The primary function of reservoirs is dominated by hydropower across the world (Fig. 2a), and the NS values of hydropower reservoirs are generally higher than those of others (Fig. 2b–d). We calculated the storage capacity percentage of hydropower reservoirs for each basin. Then, we analyzed the correlation between these three drivers and the long-term mean NS values (2000–2018) at the basin scale (Fig. 5). Note that a log-log transformation was applied for the evaluation of the runoff and population density to correct for heteroskedasticity. 

Runoff varies greatly across global basins, with low values in Central Asia, southern Africa, and Oceania; and high values in the tropical regions and South Asia (Fig. 5a). As shown in Fig. 5b, the longterm mean runoff and NS values show a significant positive correlation (Pearson correlation r = 0.21, p < 0.05). The East and South Asia regions are the most densely populated, represented by China and India (Fig. 5c). Conversely, the high-latitude regions, the Amazon, and Oceania are each sparsely populated (Fig. 5c). As indicated in Fig.

5d, population density is significantly correlated with the NS pattern (r = −0.36, p < 0.001). We used the storage capacity percentage of hydropower reservoirs for evaluating the role of reservoir function, as hydropower reservoirs need to maintain relatively high water levels to ensure that their generators operate efficiently. Figure 5e shows the storage capacity percentage of the hydropower reservoirs within each basin. The reservoirs in the high-latitude basins are primarily designed for hydropower (and therefore have high hydropower percentages), while the basins in sub-tropical regions have relatively low hydropower percentages. However, the basins in South America and central Africa also have high hydropower percentages. The significantly positive correlation (Fig. 5f) between hydropower percentage and NS (r = 0.37, p < 0.001) indicates that reservoir function is also an important driver of NS level.

reviewer_spans.text: ## Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):

I have carefully reviewed the author’s revision. The authors have taken additional effort to address my technical concerns. Particularly, I was concerned about the global applicability of the authors’ method in modeling reservoir bathymetric profiles. Accordingly, the authors have expanded the validation of the profile modeling method to the 347 reservoirs included in the Global Reservoir Bathymetry Dataset (GRBD). The modeled reservoir storage capacities agree overall well with the storage capacities based on reservoir bathymetries in GRBD. I was also concerned about the impacts of ignoring reservoir sedimentation on the derived Normalized Storage (NS) trend. Accordingly, the authors expanded the discussion on the theoretical impact of reservoir sedimentation, accompanied by an experiment on four US reservoirs. Their discussion shows that ignoring sedimentation may underestimate the severity of the NS decline, but the underestimation is probably small. The authors have also included some of the validation statistics to the uncertainties of their trend estimates.

I found the authors’ revision has further improved the fidelity of their data products and the reliability of their scientific results. While this is encouraging, I reserve a few technical concerns and remain skeptical about what’s really behind the pattern of declining reservoir NS. In addition, I found the connotation of “diminishing returns of reservoir construction” rather implicit. This is partially because the current attribution, which is based on simple correlation analysis, has not yet sufficiently disentangled the signals of climate, reservoir construction, and operations/managements. I listed my remaining concerns below for the authors to further consider.

R2C3. Impact of reservoir sedimentation. The authors rebutted that their conclusions based on reservoir NS are not affected by the ignorance of reservoir sedimentation, because “sedimentation tends to reduce the actual storage (numerator) and storage capacity (denominator) equally”. I agree with this rebuttal, if we assume sediment infilling did not affect the states of reservoir surface water elevation or area in the first place. This assumption may be true when the total sediment in a reservoir does not exceed the sediment reserve or the dead pool storage. But in other cases, substantial sediment infilling might lead to an altered operation of the reservoir water stage, which consequentially affected the reservoir water area. For instance, the reservoir conservation pool allows some flexibility to elevate the water level to compensate for the loss of actual water storage due to infilling, although this depends on the sedimentation adaptation policy of the reservoir. I am not sure how common this case occurred in aging reservoirs. Can the authors double check from the literature or at least include some discussion? In summary, I am concerned that, if the average water level of an aging reservoir was elevated as a response to sedimentation, the water area time series mapped from spectral images would also be enlarged, which could lead to an overestimated phase (or a positive bias) of the NS time series in the pre1999 reservoirs.

R2C7. Validation of the reservoir bathymetric profile models. This expanded validation, which included 347 reservoirs with detailed bathymetry in GRBD, still focuses on total reservoir storage capacity, NOT the NS trend that matters more to the authors’ scientific conclusions. Since the profile model selection was gauged by storage capacity, it is not too surprising that the modeled storage capacities agree well with those in GRBD. However, I am not sure the agreement in storage capacity also warrants a good agreement between the NS trends derived from the two methods. As I suggested previously, I strongly encourage the authors to go further and conduct a more comprehensive comparison between the results (not only storage capacities but also NS trends) based on the profile modeling method and the results based on GRBD bathymetries. I see this additional validation very important for justifying and assuring a global applicability of the authors’ modeling method.

R2C10. Reservoir water area at capacity. Based on the equations in Extended Data Table 2, the water area at capacity (Ao) functions as a scaling factor and is critical to the accuracies of the derived storage change and NS time series. In general, an overestimated Ao would lead to a

negative bias of the NS time series, and vice versa. For this reason, I have been critical about whether the authors estimated Ao for pre-1999 and post-1999 reservoirs consistently, and particularly, whether there is a possibility that the values of Ao for pre-1999 reservoirs were “underestimated” in comparison with those for post-1999 ones. If so, the higher phase of the NS time series in the pre-1999 reservoirs (a key finding of this paper) would be, in part, an artefact of the scaling bias.

As the authors clarified in the rebuttal, “if the 95th percentile area was less than the reported area in GRanD, the maximum documented area value was selected to represent the area at capacity”, and “only 20% of the post-1999 reservoirs use the 95-percentile area to represent the area at capacity”. This means that for the majority (80%) of post-1999 reservoirs, the maximum area value documented in GRanD is greater than the 95-percentile area in GRSAD. This is in contrary to pre-1999 reservoirs, where the majority (roughly 75%) ended up having the value in GRanD replaced by the 95-percentile area in GRSAD to present the area at capacity (as described in Lines 263-266). This means that the maximum area available in GRanD is smaller than the 95-percentile area in GRSAD for most of the pre-1999 reservoirs.

By looking into GRanD v1.3, I noticed that for about 50% of the post-1999 reservoirs, the maximum area value in GRanD comes from the polygon area, rather than “Area_rep” or “Area_max”. As described in the technical documentation of GRanD, most new reservoir polygons added in v1.3 were based on the maximum (100-percentile) water occurrence extent of the Joint Research Center (JRC) product (Pekel et al. 2016). This perhaps explained why the authors here found the GRanD areas for most post-1999 reservoirs are already larger than the 95-percentile GRSAD areas (which were also based on the JRC occurrence product). Regardless of the reason, we here may have Ao for most pre-1999 reservoirs based on the 95-percentile area but Ao for most post-1999 reservoirs based on the water extent larger than the 95-percentile area. This inconsistency echoes my above-described concern, i.e., the decrease of NS in post-1999 reservoirs as a false signal. I recommend the authors to further examine this possibility.

Eventually, about the meaning of “diminishing returns of reservoir construction”. I still struggle to fully understand what this expression conveys scientifically, so I highly recommend that the authors explicitly define the connotation of this expression in text. Even if the above technical concerns are all cleared, the relatively low NS value and the declining NS trend in post-1999 reservoirs may not necessarily suggest new reservoir constructions are diminishing. As seen in Figure 1, post- and pre-1999 reservoirs exhibit very different spatial distributions: as the authors also mentioned, post-1999 reservoirs are more spread out whereas newer reservoirs tend to emerge in developing countries, with a major cluster in the headwater regions of southwestern China and Southeast Asia. It is completely possible that this geographic skewedness, with differences in stream power, climate, and reservoir operation rules, may have contributed to part of the difference in NS behaviors (phase, trend, and seasonal amplitude) between pre- and post1999 reservoirs. Additionally, the existing attribution analysis also indicates the NS declines in South America and Africa were probably climate-related, rather than being an impact of new reservoirs. So overall, some of the claims, such as “reservoirs constructed in the 21st century” are “more susceptible to droughts” and “the recent returns of global reservoir constructions have been declining”, appear vague and lacking logical supports.
## Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):

The authors have carefully addressed my previous comments. I reiterate the value of this study. However, while I appreciate that the authors added caveats regarding sedimentation, the analysis and additional elements provided in response to my comments and that of the other reviewer warrant adjustment.

First, P20L362 “Despite the impacts of sedimentation on the absolute reservoir storage, the conclusions based on the normalized storage (NS) results are not affected. This is because sedimentation tends to reduce the actual storage (numerator) and storage capacity (denominator) equally, so the NS is not much affected.” Although the statement that NS is unaffected is valid, this strict definition of NS (using current storage capacity rather than initial storage capacity as the denominator) is of little relevance for management. What really matters for water provision and hydroelectric production for example, is actual storage/initial storage capacity. Therefore, I suggest removing this argument.

Second, I question the choice of reservoirs for illustrating the impact of sedimentation. How were these reservoirs chosen? The annual sedimentation rates, which range between 0.025 and 0.253%/year are on the very low range compared to global averages. The following paragraph from Wisser et al. (2013) illustrates this point : “A global data set with consistently measured sediment volumes trapped in reservoirs over time is not available, and, in fact there has been a decline in the collection of sedimentation data [Syvitski, 2003; Vanmaercke et al., 2011b]. For the US, the Reservoir Sedimentation Database (RESSED) [Ackermann et al., 2009] provides statistics on reservoir volumes derived from bathymetric surveys for more than 1800 reservoirs from which sedimentation loss rates can be calculated (using successive surveys). We calculated sedimentation rates of 1024 reservoirs with at least two complete surveys (using the most recent surveys) and supplemented this data set with observed loss rates from an additional 191 reservoirs globally from a variety of sources (Figure 1) to get a global sample of observed loss rates.This data set covers a wide range of physical conditions in the catchment (e.g., slope, climate, soil type, and land use) and local reservoir conditions (size, area, bathymetry, purpose, and management practices). Observed loss rates vary between 0.0017% a−1 and 36% a−1 and are 1.35% a−1 on average (median = 0.55% a−1). Loss rates for reservoirs with a capacity larger than the minimum capacity in the GRanD database (1 million m3) have lower loss rates (mean = 0.76% a−1, median 0.35% a−1; Table 1). Weighted by initial capacity, the mean loss rate is 0.66%.

Out of fifty reservoirs in Italy, Patro et al. (2022) mention “According to the latest report of the International Commission On Large Dams (ICOLD, 2009), the global average value for sedimentation rate (and so storage loss) is around 0.96%.” and find mean annual sedimentation rates of 0.57% and a total mean loss of reservoir capacity of 37%.

These points do not lessen the merit of this study but must be properly acknowledged. Sedimentation is a widespread phenomenon in reservoirs that surely has, on aggregate, more long-term impact on storage capacity than the changes observed by this study.
Once these corrections are made, I consider this study to be ready for publication.

## **Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):**
We greatly appreciate your comments. They have significantly improved the manuscript. We have addressed them in the following responses, and have revised the manuscript accordingly.

R2C3. Impact of reservoir sedimentation. The authors rebutted that their conclusions based on reservoir NS are not affected by the ignorance of reservoir sedimentation, because “sedimentation tends to reduce the actual storage (numerator) and storage capacity (denominator) equally”. I agree with this rebuttal, if we assume sediment infilling did not affect the states of reservoir surface water elevation or area in the first place. This assumption may be true when the total sediment in a reservoir does not exceed the sediment reserve or the dead pool storage. But in other cases, substantial sediment infilling might lead to an altered operation of the reservoir water stage, which consequentially affected the reservoir water area. For instance, the reservoir conservation pool allows some flexibility to elevate the water level to compensate for the loss of actual water storage due to infilling, although this depends on the sedimentation adaptation policy of the reservoir. I am not sure how common this case occurred in aging reservoirs. Can the authors double check from the literature or at least include some discussion? In summary, I am concerned that, if the average water level of an aging reservoir was elevated as a response to sedimentation, the water area time series mapped from spectral images would also be enlarged, which could lead to an overestimated phase (or a positive bias) of the NS time series in the pre-1999 reservoirs.

Thanks for this comment. We have searched the literature broadly (e.g., journal papers and technical reports) but did not find explicit answers for this comment. Therefore, to find out how common this case occurs in aging reservoirs affected by sedimentation, we consulted Dagmar Llewellyn, a hydrologist and planning supervisor from Bureau of Reclamation. Such cases should be very rare, according to her response below:

“Water managers do not often change their operations in response to sediment build up in the reservoirs, and that sediment does not often change the surface area of the reservoir when it is full. There are certain circumstances in which what the reviewer is saying could occur.  For example, if a flood-control reservoir has a recreation pool for which Congress authorized a certain volume of water, which is well below the capacity of the reservoir.  In this case, yes, sedimentation could increase the surface area required to store the specified amount of water. However, I think this in an exception that proves the rule that, for most reservoirs, this would not happen - we water managers would not change our operation because of sediment at the bottom of the reservoir. I think this would almost never be done for water storage reservoirs, since generally, these reservoirs store whatever water is available, up to the capacity of the reservoir.

Sediment at the bottom of the reservoir does not allow for water to be stored higher, since the total storage is limited by the dam. Instead, the capacity of the reservoir just decreases for the same surface area. For flood control reservoirs, there is some small possibility (like in my first example), but generally the flood pools are based on specific pool elevations, which correlate with a specific surface area that does not change with accumulation of sediment at the bottom of the reservoir.”

Thanks for this comment. We compared the NS trend values derived from the simulation method with the results from bathymetry-based methods for 347 global reservoirs. Figure R1 shows that the NS trend values derived from these two methods show good agreement (R[2] = 0.76), with the majority of the points centered on the 1:1 line (with a slope value of 0.99).

R2C10. Reservoir water area at capacity. Based on the equations in Extended Data Table 2, the water area at capacity (Ao) functions as a scaling factor and is critical to the accuracies of the derived storage change and NS time series. In general, an overestimated Ao would lead to a negative bias of the NS time series, and vice versa. For this reason, I have been critical about whether the authors estimated Ao for pre-1999 and post-1999 reservoirs consistently, and particularly, whether there is a possibility that the values of Ao for pre-1999 reservoirs were “underestimated” in comparison with those for post-1999 ones. If so, the higher phase of the NS time series in the pre-1999 reservoirs (a key finding of this paper) would be, in part, an artefact of the scaling bias.

As the authors clarified in the rebuttal, “if the 95th percentile area was less than the reported area in GRanD, the maximum documented area value was selected to represent the area at capacity”, and “only 20% of the post-1999 reservoirs use the 95-percentile area to represent the area at capacity”. This means that for the majority (80%) of post-1999 reservoirs, the maximum area value documented in GRanD is greater than the 95-percentile area in GRSAD. This is in contrary to pre-1999 reservoirs, where the majority (roughly 75%) ended up having the value in GRanD

replaced by the 95-percentile area in GRSAD to present the area at capacity (as described in Lines 263-266). This means that the maximum area available in GRanD is smaller than the 95percentile area in GRSAD for most of the pre-1999 reservoirs.

By looking into GRanD v1.3, I noticed that for about 50% of the post-1999 reservoirs, the maximum area value in GRanD comes from the polygon area, rather than “Area_rep” or “Area_max”. As described in the technical documentation of GRanD, most new reservoir polygons added in v1.3 were based on the maximum (100-percentile) water occurrence extent of the Joint Research Center (JRC) product (Pekel et al. 2016). This perhaps explained why the authors here found the GRanD areas for most post-1999 reservoirs are already larger than the 95percentile GRSAD areas (which were also based on the JRC occurrence product). Regardless of the reason, we here may have Ao for most pre-1999 reservoirs based on the 95-percentile area but Ao for most post-1999 reservoirs based on the water extent larger than the 95-percentile area. This inconsistency echoes my above-described concern, i.e., the decrease of NS in post-1999 reservoirs as a false signal. I recommend the authors to further examine this possibility.

Thanks for pointing this out. We agree with the reviewer that water area at capacity (Ao) is an important input for the simulation model. It is challenging to validate the water area values due to the lack of in situ data (Zhao et al. 2018). Therefore, we used the _in situ_ storage values of the 277 reservoirs (that we used to validate our storage dataset) to conduct an uncertainty analysis, using the 95-percentile area as the water area at capacity. We used the improved simulation method to derive the storage values from 1999 to 2018, with water-area-at-capacity inputs values from the 95- and 100-percentile areas, respectively. Validation results (Figure R2a-b) indicate that the storage values from the 95- and 100-percentile area inputs agree well with the _in situ_ values (R[2] values of 0.98 and 0.99, and RMSE values of 0.30 km[3 ] and 0.29 km[3] ). In addition, we compared the storage values derived from these two inputs (Figure R2c), which show good agreement (with a slope of 1.0 and a bias of 0.015 km[3] ). This small bias should have very limited impact on the NS values at large scales, as compared to the large capacity values. Thus, our key findings are reliable by using the 95-percentile area as the water area at capacity.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):

I want to thank the authors for their continued effort improving the manuscript. I have carefully reviewed their revision for this round, and found my major concerns addressed fairly well and the manuscript further improved. I have a few more suggestions based on the authors’ responses to each of my previous concerns. Once these suggestions have been incorporated, I will feel comfortable to recommend its publication in Nature Communications.

About sedimentation impact on reservoir water level and area. I would like to thank the authors for looking into the literature and consulting Dagmar Llewellyn in the Bureau of Reclamation. I accept this rebuttal. Since potential readers may have similar concerns, I highly recommend that the authors include a similar discussion in the paper (in either the main text or methods) to echo this rebuttal.

For example, the authors can briefly discuss: (1) how reservoir management may respond to sedimentation (in most cases, sedimentation does not allow for water to be stored higher, with the exception of some of the flood-control reservoirs), and (2) how this response implies to the validity of the authors’ methods and conclusions (as sediment accumulates, the reservoir storage capacity may just decrease under the same water area, leading to limited impacts on the NS).

About validation of the NS trends. It seems the NS trends derived from the simulation method are overall comparable with the trends from the bathymetry-based method. Although there are some disagreement and variability, the mean bias between the two methods appears low. I think this is a positive message. I highly recommend the authors add this validation (with Figure R1) to the paper (such as in “Evaluation of storage estimation” section), because given the focus here, validating NS trends is just as important as validating storage capacities. As another (optional) suggestion: If I were the authors, I would also try to absorb the validation statistics (such as the RMSE in Figure R1) to the uncertainties of the NS trend estimates for at least the 347 GRBD reservoirs.

About reservoir water area at capacity (Ao). It is good to see the authors have performed this sensitivity test and the difference between the estimated capacities using 95% Ao and those using 100% Ao appears limited based on the 277 reservoirs with in-situ storage. This is encouraging. To further secure this very important aspect, I am wondering if the authors can expand this sensitivity analysis to other reservoirs, in order to inform the potential impact of inconsistent use of Ao on the conclusions about pre- and post-1999 NS.

For example, I suggest the following scheme for the sensitivity analysis (which should be straightforward to implement): (1) for the subset of pre-1999 reservoirs using 95% water occurrence as Ao, replace their Ao by 100% water occurrence, (2) for the subset of post-1999 reservoirs using 95% water occurrence as Ao, keep their Ao as they are (basically do nothing for post-1999 reservoirs), and (3) compare how much difference this inconsistent use of Ao will cause for the calculated pre-1999 and post-1999 NS values. This design should, in theory, report the maximum impact of Ao. As a reminder, the authors may need to re-simulate the geometric models for some of the pre-1999 reservoirs because their Ao is changed. I also recommend that the authors include such a sensitivity analysis in the method section, which will secure to readers that this aspect won’t affect the main conclusions of the paper.

About “diminishing returns”. I want to thank the authors for clarifying the meaning of “return” and making modifications in the text. While I am still not fully convinced by some of the arguments, the changes have been much helpful and clearer. My concern is: even the same basin does not warrant a homogenous hydroclimate condition, and reservoir operation and storage pattern vary by stream power, geomorphology, and nuances in water management, which can vary reservoir by reservoir and across the same basin. So as a reader, I am not fully convinced that smaller NS values and larger seasonal variations in the post-1999 reservoirs have to suggest newer reservoirs are more susceptible to drought and brining less “return” values. I recommend that the authors give a last try to further clarity some of the terms (such as explicitly define what “return” means
as early as possible) and probably soften some of the claims lacking solid supports.
